READ FIRST, in this order — binding contract:
1. `docs/design-system.md` — tokens, components, and an AUDITED table of what does NOT exist.
2. `app/globals.css` — "KODELY PRODUCT SURFACE" and "PRODUCT UTILITIES" blocks.
3. `components/ui/*` — the primitives. Import them; never hand-roll a second version.
4. `components/app/AppShell.tsx`, `app/(portal)/layout.tsx` — your pages render CONTENT ONLY.
5. `app/(portal)/settings/page.tsx` (only 58 lines today), `app/(portal)/settings/SpendCapForm.tsx`, `lib/auth.ts`, `app/legal/rights/page.tsx`, `app/api/account/**`, `prisma/schema.prisma` (the `User` and `Session` models).

YOU OWN: everything under `app/(portal)/settings/`, plus any NEW route you need under `app/api/account/`. Do NOT touch other portal pages, `components/ui/**`, `components/app/**`, or existing `app/api/account/**` route files unless you are adding a new one alongside them.

## TASK — a properly sectioned Settings area

Today it is one 58-line page. Split it into real sections with sub-navigation (tabs or a settings sub-nav — your call, justify it). Do not dump everything on one giant page.

### What is REAL today — wire all of it up properly

- **Spend cap** — `app/(portal)/settings/SpendCapForm.tsx`, `app/api/account/spend-cap/route.ts`. Real.
- **Rewards** — `components/rewards/RewardsCard.tsx`, renders nothing when unconfigured. Real, conditionally.
- **Delete account** — real, two-step with a grace period: `app/api/account/deletion/route.ts`, `.../confirm/route.ts`, `app/api/account/_deletion.ts`. **Currently it lives at `/legal/rights`, NOT in Settings.** It belongs in a Danger Zone here. Do not duplicate the logic — surface the existing flow. Decide whether `/legal/rights` keeps its copy (it probably should, for the legal route) and say what you chose.
- **Data export** — real, streamed JSON: `app/api/account/export/route.ts`. Same situation as above.
- **Email** — readable, display only. There is no change-email route; do not build a field that silently does nothing.

### Two things that are NOT built but ARE cheaply real — build them

1. **Editing `User.name`.** The field exists (`prisma/schema.prisma:22`) and is written at signup and in the Google callback, but there is NO edit path. Add a real one: a route under `app/api/account/`, validated, length-capped, and wired to the form. The name is already used across the portal ("Welcome back, <name>"), so this genuinely matters.

2. **Active sessions list + revoke.** The `Session` model (`prisma/schema.prisma:243-253`) is per-user and fully queryable, but nothing lists or revokes them — logout only kills the current one (`lib/auth.ts:50-55`). The audit called this "the cheapest real feature on the list". Build it: list the customer's sessions, mark the current one, allow revoking others and revoking all. Be careful and correct about which session is the current one, and about not letting someone lock themselves out in a confusing way.

**Read the `Session` model and `lib/auth.ts` carefully first.** If the model does not record enough to describe a session usefully to a human (created date, last seen, user agent, IP), then say exactly what it does and does not record and show only what is true — a session row labelled with invented device details would be worse than a bare timestamp. If you add a field to the schema, note that `prisma db push` has NOT been run and flag it clearly in your report.

### What does NOT exist — do not fake any of it

Avatar upload (no field, no storage) · password change/reset (no route writes `passwordHash` after signup) · 2FA · notification preferences (`lib/notifications/templates.ts:20-21` says outright there is no consent record and no unsubscribe mechanism; the four notification kinds are transactional) · login history (`LoginAttempt` stores hashed buckets *deliberately* without identity, so it can never be shown as "your logins") · workspace / members / roles / invitations (there is no workspace concept anywhere — ownership is one FK, `Project.userId`).

For each of these, decide: omit it entirely, or show it with `EmptyState kind="unavailable"` saying plainly what is missing. Security section in particular should not look empty — sessions and account deletion are real and belong there. Justify your choices in the report.

HARD RULES:
- **Never build something that only pretends to work.**
- No new npm dependencies. Server Components by default; `"use client"` only where interaction needs it.
- `k-focus` on every interactive element, `k-num` on figures.
- Any new API route must check auth itself, validate input, and follow the patterns in the existing `app/api/account/` routes exactly (read two of them before writing one).
- Harden params with `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call` — never `x in OBJ`.
- Must pass `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint` on your paths with ZERO errors and ZERO warnings.

REPORT BACK: what you built, exactly what `Session` records and what you therefore could and could not show, which unavailable items you omitted vs surfaced and why, any schema change (flagged loudly), and anything untested.

1	# Kodely product design system
2	
3	The contract for the customer-facing portal (`app/(portal)/**`) and the builder
4	(`app/projects/[id]/**`). Marketing pages (`app/page.tsx`, `/pricing`, `/blog`,
5	`/templates`, `/wizard`) are a **separate** system — do not repoint their tokens.
6	
7	## The one-sentence brief
8	
9	An AI website builder that happens to have a customer portal around it — not a
10	dashboard that happens to contain a builder. The primary action is always
11	"build something".
12	
13	---
14	
15	## Tokens
16	
17	Defined in `app/globals.css`, exposed to Tailwind via `@theme inline`. **Use the
18	Tailwind class, never a raw hex and never an arbitrary-value bracket.**
19	
20	### Surface
21	
22	| Class | Use |
23	| --- | --- |
24	| `bg-canvas` | The page behind panels. Set by `AppShell`; pages never set it. |
25	| `bg-surface` | Cards, panels, the sidebar. |
26	| `bg-surface-2` | Hover, inset rows, quiet fills. |
27	| `bg-surface-3` | Track of a progress bar, the deepest step. |
28	| `bg-inset` | Code/preview wells. |
29	
30	### Line
31	
32	`border-hair` (default for cards) · `border-line-mid` (inputs, menus) ·
33	`border-line-strong` (emphasis, pending step outline)
34	
35	### Text
36	
37	`text-ink` (primary) · `text-ink-2` (secondary/body) · `text-ink-3` (tertiary,
38	placeholder, disabled) · `text-ink-inv` (on a brand fill)
39	
40	### Brand
41	
42	`text-brand` `bg-brand` `bg-brand-tint` `bg-brand-tint-2` `text-brand-ink`
43	
44	`--brand-gradient` is a **fill of last resort**. Exactly one element per view may
45	carry it: the primary button. Do not gradient headings, cards, borders or icons.
46	
47	### Status
48	
49	`ok` `warn` `danger` `info`, each with a `-tint` companion
50	(`text-ok` / `bg-ok-tint`). Status colour is never the brand colour.
51	
52	### Radius / elevation / motion
53	
54	`rounded-sm|md|lg|xl|2xl` (8/10/14/20/28px) · `shadow-e1|e2|e3` ·
55	`duration-[var(--t-1)]` 120ms, `--t-2` 200ms, `--t-3` 380ms ·
56	`ease-[var(--ease)]`
57	
58	---
59	
60	## Utility classes
61	
62	`k-focus` — **put this on every interactive element.** One focus ring, product-wide.
63	`k-display` `k-h1` `k-h2` `k-label` — the type scale. `k-label` is the only uppercase.
64	`k-num` — **required** on any figure: credits, prices, counts, dates in a column.
65	`k-scroll-x` — wrap any wide table/code block. The page body must never scroll sideways.
66	`k-msg-in` `k-step-in` `k-step-active` — entrance and progress animations.
67	`k-preview-busy` / `k-preview-idle` — the preview treatment while the AI works.
68	`k-wash` — ambient brand glow inside a hero panel. Sparingly: one per page, at most.
69	`k-gradient-border` — gradient hairline. Reserve for the single most important panel.
70	
71	---
72	
73	## Components (`components/ui/`)
74	
75	Import these. **Do not hand-roll a second version of any of them.**
76	
77	| Component | Notes |
78	| --- | --- |
79	| `Button` `ButtonLink` `IconButton` `buttonClass` | Variants `primary\|secondary\|ghost\|soft\|danger`, sizes `xs\|sm\|md\|lg`. **One `primary` per view.** `IconButton` requires `label`. |
80	| `Card` `CardHeader` `SectionHeader` | `interactive` only if it truly responds. |
81	| `Badge` | `tone` + `dot` + `pulse`. Set `dot` on anything conveying live state — colour alone is not a status channel. |
82	| `Input` `Textarea` `Select` `SearchInput` | Label/hint/error/aria wiring is built in. Never hand-write a bare `<input>`. |
83	| `Progress` `toneForUsage` | Recolours as it fills. `indeterminate` for work with no known end. |
84	| `Skeleton` `SkeletonList` | Stagger with `delay`. |
85	| `EmptyState` | `kind` is required: `empty` (none yet) / `no-results` (filter too narrow) / `unavailable` (does not exist yet). These need different sentences. |
86	| `Menu` | Keyboard + Escape + click-outside already handled. `unavailableReason` greys an item and says why. |
87	| `Modal` `ConfirmModal` | Native `<dialog>`. Confirm buttons are labelled with the verb, never "OK". |
88	| `ToastProvider` `useToast` | Provider is already mounted by `AppShell`. Errors and toasts with an action do not auto-dismiss. |
89	| `Segmented` | Real radios. Used for grid/list and device toggles. |
90	| `AIProgress` `stepsAt` | **The** progress component. See below. |
91	| `Stat` `StatRow` | Any number the customer must understand. |
92	| `Avatar` | Initials only — there is no avatar upload. |
93	| `Spinner` | |
94	
95	## Shell (`components/app/`)
96	
97	`AppShell` wraps every portal page and already provides the sidebar, mobile
98	drawer, bottom bar and toast host. **A page renders content only** — no page
99	supplies its own nav, no page sets a background, no page mounts a second
100	`ToastProvider`.
101	
102	Navigation lives in `components/app/nav.ts`. An item may only be added there
103	once it is backed by real data; `soon: true` marks the ones that are not.
104	
105	---
106	
107	## AI progress is one object, not three spinners
108	
109	`AIProgress` is rendered by the initial build overlay, by the chat panel during
110	an edit, and beside the preview. All three must show the **same steps in the
111	same state**, because the customer reads them as one thing happening.
112	
113	**Drive `state` from real build signals.** A timer that walks the list forward on
114	its own is a fake — and it will still be sitting on "Finalizing" long after a
115	build has failed. The build genuinely does not know its percentage (it is an
116	agent loop of unknown length), which is exactly why this is a named-step list
117	and not a progress bar.
118	
119	---
120	
121	## What does not exist (audited — do not build UI that pretends otherwise)
122	
123	| Thing | Reality |
124	| --- | --- |
125	| **Plans / subscriptions** | None. No plan, price, or renewal date. Checkout is one-off `payment` mode for credit packs. **Never render a "Pro" chip or "$X/month".** |
126	| **Credit reset date** | Credits never expire. There is no monthly allowance and no reset day — the spend cap is a *rolling* 30 days chosen so there is no reset. |
127	| **Invoices / payment method** | Not fetched from Stripe. The credit ledger is the only history. |
128	| **Thumbnails** | Nothing captures a screenshot. No headless browser. |
129	| **Project status** | Only `publishedAt` → Published / Draft. No `archived`. "Building" is derivable from `Build.status = RUNNING` but has no staleness rule, so it is not yet trustworthy. |
130	| **Domains** | No model, no field, no route. Sites live at `<slug>.kodely.site` only. |
131	| **Integrations** | Nothing customer-facing. |
132	| **Support tickets** | No ticket model. `SupportNote` is admin-write-only and explicitly never shown to the customer. |
133	| **Storage / bandwidth** | Not measured anywhere. |
134	| **Workspaces / members / roles** | No concept of it. Ownership is one FK: `Project.userId`. |
135	| **Avatar upload, password change, 2FA, notification prefs** | None. |
136	
137	**Sessions list and revoke, and editing `User.name`, ARE cheaply real** — the
138	`Session` model is per-user and queryable.
139	
140	### The rule
141	
142	A screen that looks operable and is not is worse than an absent one. A screen
143	that says "this does not exist yet, here is what you have instead" is neither.
144	Use `EmptyState kind="unavailable"` and say plainly what is missing.
145

1	import { db } from "@/lib/db";
2	
3	// ── Self-service account deletion (an erasure request) ────────────────────
4	//
5	// Two things make this file longer than "delete the user row" — both of them
6	// deliberate.
7	//
8	// WHY THIS IS A REQUEST WITH A GRACE PERIOD, NOT A BUTTON. Erasure here is
9	// irreversible: there is no soft-delete column anywhere in the schema and no
10	// backup restore path a support agent could reach for. A single click that
11	// destroys someone's work is also a single click an attacker who has stolen a
12	// session can make on their behalf. So a request is recorded, the account
13	// keeps working untouched, the owner is emailed, and nothing is destroyed
14	// until a second, explicit confirmation after DELETION_GRACE_DAYS.
15	//
16	// WHY THE USER ROW SURVIVES ERASURE. `CreditLedger.userId` is
17	// ON DELETE CASCADE, so `db.user.delete()` takes the ledger with it. Three
18	// concrete things break if it does:
19	//
20	//   1. lib/retention.ts NEVER_PRUNED commits, in writing, that the ledger is
21	//      "an auditable financial record ... Retained permanently", and every
22	//      balance in the product is derived from it rather than stored.
23	//   2. app/api/rewards/_lib.ts enforces one reward grant per EXTERNAL account
24	//      by scanning ledger `reason` strings across all users
25	//      (identityAlreadyUsed). Cascading those rows away makes "delete the
26	//      account, sign up again, reconnect the same Discord" an unlimited credit
27	//      farm — real model spend, roughly $0.40 an account, minted by a loop.
28	//   3. Purchase rows carry `stripe:<checkout_session_id>`, which is the record
29	//      of money actually received.
30	//
31	// So erasure destroys every piece of personal content and STRIPS the account
32	// row down to a tombstone — no email, no name, no Google id, no Stripe
33	// customer id, no password — leaving the ledger attached to an id that no
34	// longer resolves to a person. The rows that remain are a delta, a reason, a
35	// balance and a timestamp.
36	//
37	// The right long-term fix is a schema change this file is not allowed to make:
38	// `CreditLedger.userId` should be nullable and ON DELETE SET NULL, exactly as
39	// `CreditLedger.buildId` already is, at which point the User row can genuinely
40	// be deleted and the ledger simply detaches. See the report.
41	
42	/**
43	 * How long a request sits before it can be carried out.
44	 *
45	 * Long enough that a rash decision, or one made from a session someone else
46	 * controls, can be caught and cancelled — the owner is emailed the moment a
47	 * request is made. Short enough that "we will delete your account" does not
48	 * read as a stall.
49	 */
50	export const DELETION_GRACE_DAYS = 7;
51	
52	/** Typed by the user at BOTH steps. Case-sensitive, and deliberately not the word "yes". */
53	export const CONFIRMATION_PHRASE = "DELETE MY ACCOUNT";
54	
55	export const PRIVACY_EMAIL = "privacy@kodely.me";
56	
57	// ── Where the request is stored ───────────────────────────────────────────
58	//
59	// In SupportNote, as marker-prefixed rows. This needs explaining, because it
60	// is not what that table was built for.
61	//
62	// There is no `User.deletionRequestedAt` column and this change is not allowed
63	// to add one. The alternatives were weighed:
64	//
65	//   * CreditLedger delta-0 rows — the pattern app/api/rewards/_lib.ts already
66	//     uses for pending claims. Rejected: account lifecycle is not money, and
67	//     the row would surface in the customer's own billing history.
68	//   * The Event table — explicitly rejected by its own contract (lib/events.ts:
69	//     a closed vocabulary the privacy policy is written from) and by the same
70	//     reasoning in lib/rate-limit.ts.
71	//   * EmailLog — its unique (kind, dedupeKey) means a cancelled request could
72	//     never be re-made.
73	//
74	// SupportNote is the only per-user, timestamped, append-only table left, and a
75	// deletion request is a thing an operator genuinely should see when they open
76	// an account. The cost, stated plainly: these rows appear in the operator-notes
77	// UI, which labels itself "operator-written, never customer-facing", and one
78	// of them is neither. A `deletionRequestedAt` column removes the whole
79	// awkwardness and is the recommended follow-up.
80	//
81	// State is the LATEST marker row, the way the reward state machine is the
82	// latest matching ledger row. Nothing is ever updated or deleted to change
83	// state; a cancellation is a new row.
84	
85	const MARKER_REQUESTED = "[deletion-requested]";
86	const MARKER_CANCELLED = "[deletion-cancelled]";
87	const MARKER_COMPLETED = "[deletion-completed]";
88	
89	const MARKERS = [MARKER_REQUESTED, MARKER_CANCELLED, MARKER_COMPLETED];
90	
91	export type DeletionStatus =
92	  | { state: "none" }
93	  | {
94	      /** Requested; the grace period is still running. Cancellable. */
95	      state: "pending";
96	      requestedAt: Date;
97	      scheduledFor: Date;
98	      hoursLeft: number;
99	    }
100	  | {
101	      /** Grace period elapsed. One confirmation away from erasure. Still cancellable. */
102	      state: "due";
103	      requestedAt: Date;
104	      scheduledFor: Date;
105	    }
106	  | { state: "erased"; erasedAt: Date };
107	
108	function scheduledFrom(requestedAt: Date): Date {
109	  return new Date(requestedAt.getTime() + DELETION_GRACE_DAYS * 86_400_000);
110	}
111	
112	/**
113	 * The current state of this account's deletion request, if any.
114	 *
115	 * Scoped by userId in the same query as everything else it filters on, so it
116	 * can never read another account's markers.
117	 */
118	export async function deletionStatus(userId: string): Promise<DeletionStatus> {
119	  const latest = await db.supportNote.findFirst({
120	    where: { userId, OR: MARKERS.map((marker) => ({ body: { startsWith: marker } })) },
121	    // Id breaks a timestamp tie. Cancelling and immediately re-requesting can
122	    // land two markers in the same millisecond, and "latest wins" has to mean
123	    // something definite when it does — cuids sort by generation time, so the
124	    // newer row wins either way round.
125	    orderBy: [{ createdAt: "desc" }, { id: "desc" }],
126	    select: { body: true, createdAt: true },
127	  });
128	
129	  if (!latest) return { state: "none" };
130	
131	  if (latest.body.startsWith(MARKER_COMPLETED)) {
132	    return { state: "erased", erasedAt: latest.createdAt };
133	  }
134	  if (latest.body.startsWith(MARKER_CANCELLED)) return { state: "none" };
135	
136	  const requestedAt = latest.createdAt;
137	  const scheduledFor = scheduledFrom(requestedAt);
138	  const msLeft = scheduledFor.getTime() - Date.now();
139	  if (msLeft <= 0) return { state: "due", requestedAt, scheduledFor };
140	
141	  return {
142	    state: "pending",
143	    requestedAt,
144	    scheduledFor,
145	    // Computed server-side so the page renders the same number on the server
146	    // and on hydration, the way rewardStatuses does it.
147	    hoursLeft: Math.ceil(msLeft / 3_600_000),
148	  };
149	}
150	
151	/**
152	 * What erasure would destroy, counted before it happens.
153	 *
154	 * Shown in the confirmation UI. A dialog that says "this cannot be undone"
155	 * without saying what "this" is asks for consent to something unstated.
156	 */
157	export type DeletionPreview = {
158	  projects: number;
159	  liveSites: number;
160	  files: number;
161	  messages: number;
162	  builds: number;
163	  sessions: number;
164	  analyticsEvents: number;
165	  supportNotes: number;
166	  emailsSent: number;
167	  /** Retained, not destroyed. */
168	  creditLedgerRows: number;
169	  creditBalance: number;
170	};
171	
172	export async function deletionPreview(userId: string): Promise<DeletionPreview> {
173	  const [
174	    projects,
175	    liveSites,
176	    files,
177	    messages,
178	    builds,
179	    sessions,
180	    analyticsEvents,
181	    supportNotes,
182	    emailsSent,
183	    creditLedgerRows,
184	    newestLedgerRow,
185	  ] = await Promise.all([
186	    db.project.count({ where: { userId } }),
187	    db.project.count({ where: { userId, publishedAt: { not: null } } }),
188	    db.projectFile.count({ where: { project: { userId } } }),
189	    db.message.count({ where: { project: { userId } } }),
190	    db.build.count({ where: { project: { userId } } }),
191	    db.session.count({ where: { userId } }),
192	    db.event.count({ where: { userId } }),
193	    // The markers this module writes live in the same table, so they are
194	    // excluded from the count a person is shown — otherwise requesting
195	    // deletion would appear to create a support note about themselves.
196	    // NOT wraps a single OR rather than taking an array: `NOT: [a, b]` means
197	    // NOT(a AND b), which is vacuously true here because no body can start
198	    // with two markers at once — it would silently filter nothing.
199	    db.supportNote.count({
200	      where: { userId, NOT: { OR: MARKERS.map((marker) => ({ body: { startsWith: marker } })) } },
201	    }),
202	    db.emailLog.count({ where: { userId } }),
203	    db.creditLedger.count({ where: { userId } }),
204	    db.creditLedger.findFirst({
205	      where: { userId },
206	      orderBy: { createdAt: "desc" },
207	      select: { balanceAfter: true },
208	    }),
209	  ]);
210	
211	  return {
212	    projects,
213	    liveSites,
214	    files,
215	    messages,
216	    builds,
217	    sessions,
218	    analyticsEvents,
219	    supportNotes,
220	    emailsSent,
221	    creditLedgerRows,
222	    creditBalance: newestLedgerRow?.balanceAfter ?? 0,
223	  };
224	}
225	
226	/** Record a request. Destroys nothing. */
227	export async function requestDeletion(
228	  userId: string,
229	  requesterEmail: string,
230	): Promise<{ ok: true; status: DeletionStatus } | { ok: false; reason: "already_open" | "erased" }> {
231	  const current = await deletionStatus(userId);
232	  if (current.state === "erased") return { ok: false, reason: "erased" };
233	  if (current.state !== "none") return { ok: false, reason: "already_open" };
234	
235	  const scheduledFor = scheduledFrom(new Date());
236	
237	  await db.supportNote.create({
238	    data: {
239	      userId,
240	      // Every other row in this table is written by an operator. This one is
241	      // written by the account holder, and says so rather than borrowing a
242	      // staff address it did not come from.
243	      authorEmail: requesterEmail,
244	      body:
245	        `${MARKER_REQUESTED} The account holder requested deletion of this account from ` +
246	        `/legal/rights. Nothing is deleted before ${scheduledFor.toISOString()}, and the ` +
247	        `request can be cancelled by the account holder until it is carried out.`,
248	    },
249	  });
250	
251	  return { ok: true, status: await deletionStatus(userId) };
252	}
253	
254	/** Withdraw an open request. */
255	export async function cancelDeletion(userId: string): Promise<boolean> {
256	  const current = await deletionStatus(userId);
257	  if (current.state !== "pending" && current.state !== "due") return false;
258	
259	  await db.supportNote.create({
260	    data: {
261	      userId,
262	      authorEmail: PRIVACY_EMAIL,
263	      body: `${MARKER_CANCELLED} The account holder cancelled their deletion request. Nothing was deleted.`,
264	    },
265	  });
266	  return true;
267	}
268	
269	/** What erasure actually did. Returned to the user, and worth keeping in a log. */
270	export type ErasureReceipt = {
271	  erasedAt: string;
272	  projectsDeleted: number;
273	  liveSitesWithdrawn: number;
274	  filesDeleted: number;
275	  messagesDeleted: number;
276	  buildsDeleted: number;
277	  sessionsEnded: number;
278	  analyticsEventsDetached: number;
279	  supportNotesDeleted: number;
280	  emailRecordsDeleted: number;
281	  creditLedgerRowsRetained: number;
282	  moderationFindingsRetained: number;
283	};
284	
285	/**
286	 * Carry out the erasure. Irreversible.
287	 *
288	 * Everything happens in one transaction: an account half-erased — projects
289	 * gone but the email still on file, or the reverse — is worse than either
290	 * outcome. The timeout is raised well above Prisma's 5s default because
291	 * deleting projects cascades file trees and build snapshots, which is the
292	 * slowest write in the product.
293	 *
294	 * Callers MUST have checked `deletionStatus` is "due" first; this function
295	 * does not re-check, so that the routes own the policy and this owns the
296	 * mechanics.
297	 */
298	export async function eraseAccount(userId: string): Promise<ErasureReceipt> {
299	  const before = await deletionPreview(userId);
300	  const erasedAt = new Date();
301	
302	  const moderationFindingsRetained = await (async () => {
303	    const projects = await db.project.findMany({ where: { userId }, select: { id: true } });
304	    if (projects.length === 0) return 0;
305	    // ModerationFinding has no relation to Project in the schema, so it is not
306	    // cascaded by anything and cannot be scoped by a relation filter. It is
307	    // also deliberately NOT deleted — see the note below the transaction.
308	    return db.moderationFinding.count({
309	      where: { projectId: { in: projects.map((p) => p.id) } },
310	    });
311	  })();
312	
313	  await db.$transaction(
314	    async (tx) => {
315	      // Projects first. This is what takes a published site offline: the
316	      // cascade removes the `published: true` rows the public site route
317	      // serves AND the Project row it resolves the slug by, so
318	      // <slug>.kodely.site 404s. An already-cached page can survive up to a
319	      // minute at the CDN, which is the same caveat project deletion carries.
320	      //
321	      // The cascade also removes ProjectFile, Message and Build (including
322	      // every prompt and every filesSnapshot). CreditLedger.buildId is
323	      // ON DELETE SET NULL, so ledger rows survive with buildId cleared —
324	      // exactly what deleting a project already does today.
325	      await tx.project.deleteMany({ where: { userId } });
326	
327	      // Signed out everywhere, immediately.
328	      await tx.session.deleteMany({ where: { userId } });
329	
330	      // Operator notes are prose written about a real person. Erasure is
331	      // precisely the moment they should go — including the marker rows this
332	      // module wrote, which is why the tombstone below is created afterwards.
333	      await tx.supportNote.deleteMany({ where: { userId } });
334	
335	      // "We emailed this person" is a record about the person. Its only
336	      // function is exactly-once delivery, and nothing can be delivered to an
337	      // erased account: every notification in lib/notifications is triggered
338	      // by activity inside a 15-minute slot, and an erased account produces
339	      // none.
340	      await tx.emailLog.deleteMany({ where: { userId } });
341	
342	      // Detached, not deleted — the behaviour the schema already declares
343	      // (Event.userId is ON DELETE SET NULL) and the privacy policy already
344	      // describes. Done explicitly because the User row is not being deleted.

Welcome to the Next.js documentation!

## What is Next.js?

Next.js is a React framework for building full-stack web applications. You use React Components to build user interfaces, and Next.js for additional features and optimizations.

It also automatically configures lower-level tools like bundlers and compilers. You can instead focus on building your product and shipping quickly.

Whether you're an individual developer or part of a larger team, Next.js can help you build interactive, dynamic, and fast React applications.

## How to use the docs

The docs are organized into 3 sections:

- [Getting Started](/docs/app/getting-started): Step-by-step tutorials to help you create a new application and learn the core Next.js features.
- [Guides](/docs/app/guides): Tutorials on specific use cases, choose what's relevant to you.
- [API Reference](/docs/app/api-reference): Detailed technical reference for every feature.

Use the sidebar to navigate through the sections, or search (`Ctrl+K` or `Cmd+K`) to quickly find a page.

## App Router and Pages Router

Next.js has two different routers:

- **App Router**: The newer router that supports new React features like Server Components.
- **Pages Router**: The original router, still supported and being improved.

At the top of the sidebar, you'll notice a dropdown menu that allows you to switch between the [App Router](/docs/app) and the [Pages Router](/docs/pages) docs.

### React version handling

The App Router and Pages Router handle React versions differently:

- **App Router**: Uses [React canary releases](https://react.dev/blog/2023/05/03/react-canaries) built-in, which include all the stable React 19 changes, as well as newer features being validated in frameworks, prior to a new React release.

- **Pages Router**: Uses the React version installed in your project's `package.json`.

This approach ensures new React features work reliably in the App Router while maintaining backwards compatibility for existing Pages Router applications.

## Pre-requisite knowledge

Our documentation assumes some familiarity with web development. Before getting started, it'll help if you're comfortable with:

- HTML
- CSS
- JavaScript
- React

If you're new to React or need a refresher, we recommend starting with our [React Foundations course](/learn/react-foundations), and the [Next.js Foundations course](/learn/dashboard-app) that has you building an application as you learn.

## Accessibility

For the best experience when using a screen reader, we recommend using Firefox and NVDA, or Safari and VoiceOver.

## Join our Community

If you have questions about anything related to Next.js, you're always welcome to ask our community on [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions), [Discord](https://discord.com/invite/bUG2bvbtHy), [X (Twitter)](https://x.com/nextjs), and [Reddit](https://www.reddit.com/r/nextjs).

Everything type-checks and lints clean on my paths. Here's the report.

## What I built

**Settings is now four routed sections behind a tab bar** (`app/(portal)/settings/layout.tsx` + `SettingsNav.tsx`), not one page:

- `/settings` — **Account**: display name (editable), email (read-only), member-since, email-preferences unavailability.
- `/settings/credits` — **Credits**: spend cap with a real usage bar, plus the rewards card.
- `/settings/security` — **Security**: how you sign in, active sessions, data export, danger zone.

**Real routes, not client tabs**, because each section's queries are expensive and section-specific (Security runs the session list *and* `deletionPreview`'s eleven counts across nine tables; Credits aggregates 30 days of ledger). Client tabs would run all of it on every visit to render one panel, and would break deep-linking — which matters, see the Discord note below.

### New API routes (both auth-check themselves, validate, and mirror the existing `app/api/account/` shape)

- `app/api/account/profile/route.ts` — `GET` + `PUT { name }`. Validation lives in `app/api/account/_profile.ts` (shared with the form so client and server agree on the cap): 80 code points max, whitespace collapsed, control characters / zero-width / **bidi-override characters stripped** (the name renders inline in "Welcome back, ‹name›", and an unterminated RLO reverses the rest of the line — React escapes markup, not text direction). `""` and `null` both clear it. Body parsed with `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call`, never `in`.
- `app/api/account/sessions/route.ts` — `GET` list, `DELETE` with three shapes: `{id}` (one other session), `{scope:"others"}`, `{scope:"all"}`. `{id}` equal to the caller's own session is refused with a 409 that names the alternative rather than silently signing them out. `"all"` deletes every row *and* clears the cookie via `destroySession()` (the deletion/confirm route's pattern), returns `signedOut: true`, and the client `router.replace("/login")`s. Every `WHERE` repeats the session's own `userId`, so another account's session id is indistinguishable from one that doesn't exist. Sending both `id` and `scope`, or neither, is a 400.

## What `Session` actually records — and what I therefore could not show

```
id · userId · tokenHash (SHA-256) · expiresAt · createdAt
```

That's the whole row, and `lib/auth.ts` writes nothing else. **No user agent, no IP, no last-seen, no device, no location, and nothing joins to it.** So each row shows exactly three true things: when the sign-in happened, when it expires, and whether it's this browser. The card says so out loud — that Kodely doesn't store the browser/device/IP and *will not guess* — so nobody reads two dates as a truncated version of something richer.

**I did not add schema fields, deliberately** (so: no schema change, nothing to `prisma db push`):
- A UA/IP column is *new personal data*, and both `/legal/rights` and `app/api/account/export/route.ts` enumerate in writing everything the database holds — the export explicitly lists IP addresses under what is *not* included. Adding the column silently makes two published documents wrong.
- `lastSeenAt` can't be maintained without a DB **write on every authenticated request**, since `getCurrentUser` is what every page and route calls.

Expired rows are filtered out rather than listed as "expired" — they're already inert, and inviting someone to revoke a dead credential and feel safer is the wrong outcome. List is capped at 50 newest with the true total shown alongside.

## Unavailable items: surfaced vs omitted

| Item | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Password change / reset | **Surfaced** as prose inside the real "How you sign in" card | Nothing writes `passwordHash` after signup, so there's no route to wire. A greyed-out button would imply one exists. Google-only accounts get the accurate variant: never had a password, can't be given one. |
| 2FA | **Surfaced**, one line in the same card | Same card, no separate empty box for it |
| Sign-in history | **Surfaced**, one line in the sessions card | `LoginAttempt` stores salted hashed buckets with no identity attached, on purpose — so it can never be "your sign-ins". Said where people will look for it. |
| Notification prefs | **Surfaced** as `EmptyState kind="unavailable"` on Account | Names the four transactional emails truthfully; explains there is no list, no pixel, and therefore nothing to opt out of |
| Avatar upload | **Omitted** — no affordance anywhere; `Avatar` is initials-only by contract |
| Workspaces / members / roles / invites | **Omitted entirely** | There is no workspace concept in the schema at all — ownership is one FK. An "unavailable" Team tab would advertise something the data model has never contemplated. |

## Deletion & export

`/legal/rights` **keeps its copy** — it has to work for someone who can't reach the portal, and it's the URL the deletion email points at. **No logic is duplicated**: the Settings danger zone renders `deletionStatus()` / `deletionPreview()` on the *server* from the same `_deletion.ts` module, and its three buttons call the same two routes. Only markup and confirmation wording are new. Export is the same streamed route with the 60s cooldown mirrored client-side so a double-click is greyed rather than 429'd invisibly.

## Files touched outside `app/(portal)/settings/` — flagging each

1. **`lib/auth.ts` — additive `getCurrentSession()`.** Necessary: the list must mark exactly one row "this device" and the revoke must refuse to cut its own caller off, and both need the session id `getCurrentUser` throws away. The alternative was copying `SESSION_COOKIE` and `hashToken` out of that file — a sessions screen that disagrees with the real cookie name would mark the wrong row as current. Nothing pre-existing changed.
2. **`components/rewards/RewardsCard.tsx` — restyled onto the design system.** Its only consumer is Settings; dropping a marketing-grey card into the product surface would break the token contract. **Every fetch, state transition and route is byte-for-byte unchanged** — className strings and primitives only.
3. **`app/legal/rights/page.tsx` — two factual corrections.** It said "There is no self-serve editor for your name or email address yet", which my change makes false; it now says the name is editable in Settings and the email is not. Also repointed the spend-cap link to `/settings/credits` and added a bullet for sessions. Leaving a knowingly false statement on the legal rights page seemed worse than the edit.

## Needs a follow-up (I did not touch these — they're other agents' files, and one is being edited concurrently right now)

Six call sites deep-link to `/settings` expecting the spend cap and now land on the Account tab. They should point at `/settings/credits`:
`app/(portal)/dashboard/billing/SpendCapPanel.tsx:32,66` · `app/(portal)/dashboard/new/Composer.tsx:317,325` · `app/(portal)/dashboard/page.tsx:319` · `components/onboarding/FirstRunPanel.tsx:289`. The Credits tab is one visible click away in the meantime.

Also noted, not acted on: `docs/design-system.md:137` still says sessions and name editing "ARE cheaply real" — they're now built.

## Verification

- `npx tsc --noEmit` scoped to my paths: **clean**. Repo-wide tsc has two pre-existing errors in `app/projects/[id]/Editor.tsx` and one transient one in `app/projects/[id]/preview/page.tsx` — a concurrent agent is editing that directory (file timestamps moved between two of my runs). I touched none of it. I ran `npx next typegen` to regenerate route types for the new segments.
- `npx eslint --max-warnings=0` on all changed paths: **clean**.

**Untested:** nothing was exercised against a live database or a browser — no dev server for this app was running, I had no authenticated session, and starting one risked colliding with the concurrent agent's `.next`. Specifically unverified at runtime: the revoke round-trips, the "sign out everywhere" cookie clear and redirect, the `?reward=` forward from `/settings` → `/settings/credits`, and all CSS rendering. Query shapes and props are type-checked against the generated Prisma client, and one cascade hazard was avoided deliberately (the danger zone uses `ring-danger`, not a `border-danger` override, since both would set `border-color` and stylesheet order — not attribute order — decides).
